title: Sable Systems POC - Cost & Unit Workshop
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-12-20
Time: 14:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO - Sable), Leah Kim (ML Eng), Omar Aziz (Infra), Nora Feldman (Procurement)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics (tokens/sec/$), caching and batching tradeoffs. Reviewed pilot numbers from last 72h run, confirmed KV/prefix caching cut token render costs ~27% on the user flows. Discussed need for longer 8k context bench, quantization impact, and host vs dedicated routing for tail latency. Agreed next steps: bench with cache + batched 8k runs, share updated pricing sheet, procurement to validate terms.
topics: 1) Recent 72h pilot results 2) Caching savings breakdown 3) Batching latency vs throughput tradeoffs 4) Tokens/sec per dollar calculations 5) Security and VPC implications 6) Next steps and procurement timeline
action_items: Diego Ramos: run 3x 8k-context bench with KV caching on/off and provide token/sec/$ spreadsheet - due 2026-12-24
Leah Kim: provide representative prompt set for long-context cases (10-12 prompts) - due 2026-12-22
Maya Chen: send updated pricing/pricing scenarios and Dedicated vs Hosted cost table - due 2026-12-21
Nora Feldman: confirm internal procurement timeline and any additional compliance docs needed - due 2026-12-29
next_steps: Redwood to run extended 8k context benchmarks (cache on/off, batching variations)
Redwood to share updated cost model spreadsheet and sample SLA language
Customer to validate prompt set and provide final list of 10 canonical flows
Schedule deep dive after bench results (target week of 12/27)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call — Maya here from Redwood. Diego's on the line, and from Sable we have Raj, Leah, Omar and Nora.
[00:12] Raj Patel: Hi Maya, thanks, yeah good to be here.
[00:16] Diego Ramos: afternoon all.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Goal for today — recap the last 72 hour pilot numbers, talk caching/batching tradeoffs, and agree next steps for the 8k context bench.
[00:30] Leah Kim: sounds great. we've been seeing the user flows with longer context blow out token counts––so interested in the caching numbers.
[00:38] Omar Aziz: also want to make sure we don't regress on p95 latency if we batch too aggressively. our UX team is sensitive to tail.
[00:45] Maya Chen: totally. ok Diego, can you run through the 72h run? high level numbers first.
[00:51] Diego Ramos: sure. so the run—this is the one with mixed traffic: 60% short chat-ish, 40% long-context summarization. baseline was hosted endpoint with default batching (1-16 window) and no prefix cache. Over the last 72 hours we did three variants: baseline, prefix-only cache, and full KV cache.
[01:12] Diego Ramos: baseline tokens/server-second per dollar metric — we saw about 18k tokens per $1 for the short flows, but when you include long-context summarization the blended was around 9.5k tokens per $1. With prefix caching enabled the blended improved to ~12k tokens per $1, and with KV cache it hit roughly 14.3k tokens per $1.
[01:34] Raj Patel: That’s helpful. when you say KV cache enabled, that means customer-side conversational prefix caching? or Redwood-managed prefix cache?
[01:41] Diego Ramos: good question. this was Redwood-managed KV caching at the model runtime—basically we cache key/value pairs for repeated prefixes and reuse them in the server-side inference. there might be a couple small mispronunciations in the logs, you might see K V cash in the export, but it's KV cache.
[01:56] Leah Kim: curious — how are you measuring token/sec/$ — is that averaged over the run or is it peak?
[02:02] Diego Ramos: averaged over the full-run. we also captured percentiles; peak throughput was higher but not representative of user cost. for cost modeling I usually do blended tokens/$ over X hours.
[02:13] Nora Feldman: from procurement perspective we need a worst-case cost too — like if caching misses frequently what's the delta?
[02:20] Diego Ramos: fair. in an artificial cold-cache scenario the tokens/$ dropped to about 7k tokens per $1. so worst case roughly 7k blended. but with even modest cache hit rates (25-30%) you recoup to the 10-12k range.
[02:35] Raj Patel: ok that helps quantify risk. what about batching? we worry batching hurts p95.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: so we tested 3 batching strategies: conservative (1-4), default (1-16), aggressive (1-64). conservative keeps low p95, but throughput suffers so tokens/$ is lower — about 11k for blended with cache. default is the middle ground. aggressive gives best tokens/$—we saw up to 18k blended in short flows but p95 latency would spike from 220ms to ~480ms on those long requests.
[03:05] Omar Aziz: 480ms p95 for long flows is probably too high for our interactive UI. is there a smart routing option? send latency-sensitive calls to a low-batch pool?
[03:12] Diego Ramos: yes that's exactly the smart routing policy we discussed earlier. you can route by route labels, by customer tier, or even by detected intent. route latency-sensitive routes to a low-batch pool or a dedicated low-latency model variant.
[03:24] Leah Kim: how much more expensive is the dedicated low-latency pool?
[03:28] Diego Ramos: depends on utilization. dedicated is more expensive per-hour but predictable. For our bench, routing 20% of calls to low-latency dedicated nodes increased effective cost by ~9% but improved p95 by ~60% on those calls. overall tokens/$ dipped a bit but UX improved.
[03:46] Maya Chen: quick note — that 9% is on the blended cost, not absolute cost for the dedicated nodes alone, so it’s doable depending on SLO.
[03:53] Raj Patel: ok. another area — quantization. did you test 4-bit or q4 variants?
[03:58] Diego Ramos: we did a small run with q4 and q5-ish mixed formats. q4 reduced cost by ~18% but we observed small quality deltas on long-context summarizations — some hallucination increase in the very long prompts. so there's a tradeoff: quantization → cost down, but guard rails/evals needed to ensure quality.
[04:20] Leah Kim: can you expand on the hallucination signal? how did you measure regression?
[04:24] Diego Ramos: we used a small eval set of 50 long summaries with known ground truth checks, and we tracked precision/recall style metrics plus a manual spot check. q4 had a ~4% drop on factuality checks on that sample.
[04:36] Raj Patel: ok that's a tolerable delta if the cost delta buys us scale; but we might want q4 for non-critical flows and q5 or fp16 for critical ones.
[04:45] Nora Feldman: on compliance — do the caches store any customer PII? we need to validate logs/audit.
[04:51] Maya Chen: good call. by default KV cache keys are transient and we can enable PII redaction. logs can be configured to omit full prompt text; Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for encryption and audit logs for access. we have SOC2 docs in the deck we sent earlier.
[05:06] Omar Aziz: is the private deployment option still coming in Q1? we need VPC-peered option for the pilot to meet our security posture.
[05:12] Maya Chen: Redwood Private GA's been accelerated with a couple of customers; we can do a VPC peering preview for you in early Jan. it will have KMS integrations and audit logs.
[05:22] Leah Kim: curious about cache hit patterns — what prompts are best suited? in our data the first 400 tokens differ but the second half repeats a lot.
[05:29] Diego Ramos: prefix caching helps when the beginning of the sequence repeats. KV caching helps reusing internal KV states across similar continuations even when the prefix slightly varies. with your flows we saw about 32% KV hit rate in the long-context test which generated the 14.3k tokens/$ number.
[05:45] Raj Patel: what if we do client-side prefix hashing so we send shorter canonical keys—reduce server work?
[05:50] Diego Ramos: you can, yeah. client-side canonicalization reduces server-match friction. tradeoff is more SDK work on your side and you lose some fidelity for dynamic user-specific context.
[06:01] Nora Feldman: procurement question — pricing model options: committed monthly reserved capacity vs pure usage?
[06:06] Maya Chen: both. Dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable price and throughput with a monthly commitment. Hosted usage-based is per-token with tier discounts. For pilots we usually recommend a small reserved commitment plus usage overage to keep predictability and lower unit costs.
[06:20] Nora Feldman: do you have example numbers for Sable-sized traffic? we sent the usage spreadsheet earlier but want to ensure the model fits our finance team.
[06:28] Maya Chen: Diego, you have the sample pricing scenarios?
[06:31] Diego Ramos: yes — I'll attach a scenario where with a 1 GPU reserved pool we assume 65% utilization and active caching/higher batching; that brings tokens/$ to effective 15k region for blended traffic. Without reservation blended tokens/$ drifts lower and costs per token are higher. I'll share the pricing sheet with three scenarios: baseline (hosted no reserve), hybrid (small reserve), dedicated (bigger reserve).
[06:50] Leah Kim: from an engineering standpoint we want the bench that replicates the UX: mix of 65/35 short/long, 10% high concurrency spikes, and the exact prompt set.
[06:58] Diego Ramos: yep — that's part of the next run. We'll add a cold-cache run too to show the lower bound.
[07:04] Maya Chen: can we pin down dates? Diego — can you run bench + sheet to Maya by Tuesday? that's the 24th.
[07:10] Diego Ramos: yes, I can have bench results and the tokens-per-dollar sheet by 24th.
[07:14] Leah Kim: I can send the prompt set tomorrow, 22nd.
[07:17] Nora Feldman: procurement will aim to review price scenarios by end of month, 29th ideally.
[07:22] Raj Patel: one more technical question — how do you handle KV invalidation when users edit prior messages? will that poison cache?
[07:29] Diego Ramos: good question. we expose TTL and invalidation hooks. If a prior message edits the conversation we can invalidated affected keys; worst case it falls back to re-computation. The hit ratio goes down for highly dynamic histories.
[07:41] Raj Patel: ok. cost sensitivity — what if we wanted to cap spending at $X per thousand users? can Redwood provide alerting?
[07:47] Maya Chen: yes, the console has token-level cost alerts and per-route budgets, plus programmatic webhooks. We can also automatically lower batching/force lower-quality variants when budgets approach threshold to avoid surprises.
[07:59] Omar Aziz: what's the expected impact on latency if you switch to a lower-quality quantized variant mid-flight?
[08:05] Diego Ramos: latency usually improves with smaller quantized models by about 10-20% in generation time, but quality tradeoff exists. tricky to do mid-flight without reevaluating state consistency.
[08:16] Leah Kim: are there any plans for built-in prompt caching in the SDK? would that help our client canonicalization?
[08:21] Maya Chen: we have a client-side SDK cache prototype that does canonicalization + local LRU cache, happy to include Sable in the beta.
[08:29] Nora Feldman: procurement note — we need indemnity and data residency clauses for our legal review. can you send a redlineable contract?
[08:36] Maya Chen: yes, I will share a standard enterprise contract and a redline template; legal has been told to expect Sable's redlines.
[08:42] Raj Patel: okay, this is great. can we do a short recap before we wrap?
[08:46] Maya Chen: recap: Diego will run extended 8k context bench (cache on/off, batching variations, cold-cache) and produce tokens/sec/$ sheet by 12/24. Leah will send canonical prompt set by 12/22. Maya will push updated pricing scenarios and contract templates by 12/21. Nora will confirm procurement timeline by 12/29. We'll reconvene week of 12/27 for deep dive.
[09:06] Diego Ramos: small add — I'll include quantization run results (q4 vs q5) in the bench deliverable and a short quality delta appendix.
[09:14] Raj Patel: sounds good. thanks all.
[09:17] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via the deck and I'll pop the sheet into the CRM.
[09:21] Nora Feldman: thanks. bye.
[09:23] (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription glitches: "K V cash" for KV cache, "q5-ish" sometimes written as "q5ish". There is mild crosstalk on a couple checks. The transcript includes procurement and security asks that will be handled via follow-up doc links. Links referenced: pricing_sheet_v3.xlsx (shared), SOC2-summary.pdf (sent), prompt_set_sable_v1.json (to be shared by customer).
